content: Rubella infection during early pregnancy can lead to severe outcomes such as miscarriage, fetal death, or congenital abnormalities. The use of immunoglobulins for post-exposure prophylaxis of rubella has been studied, but the available research is limited by small sample sizes and inconsistent results. National public health guidelines suggest that immunoglobulins may offer some degree of protection. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of intramuscular or intravenous administration of polyclonal immunoglobulins derived from human serum or plasma in preventing rubella and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) when given to susceptible individuals exposed to the virus before the onset of disease. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, LILACS, and Web of Science, was conducted up to August 2014. Additional searches were performed in clinical trial registries and reference lists of relevant studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and prospective controlled studies that met specific inclusion criteria. Participants had to be susceptible to rubella and exposed to the virus, and the intervention had to involve polyclonal immunoglobulins administered intramuscularly or intravenously. The review included 12 studies with a total of 430 participants, comprising seven RCTs and five controlled clinical trials (CCTs) where randomization was unclear. Participants included both children and adults, with only one study involving pregnant women. All studies were conducted in high-income countries. The quality of the included studies was moderate, with no study classified as having a low risk of bias across all criteria. An initial meta-analysis of 11 studies compared gamma-globulin (a concentrated form of polyclonal immunoglobulins) to control (saline or no treatment) for preventing rubella cases. The results favored the intervention group, with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.61 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.45 to 0.83). However, significant heterogeneity was observed (I² = 73%). Subgroup analyses revealed that the effectiveness of gamma-globulin was influenced by the volume administered per pound of body weight and the timing of administration. Greater effectiveness was observed when higher volumes of gamma-globulin were used and when the intervention was administered within five days of exposure. No studies reported on the outcome of congenital rubella infection. One study addressed congenital rubella syndrome, finding no cases among participants who were fewer than nine weeks pregnant at enrollment and who received gamma-globulin. However, this study did not include a non-treatment group, did not specify how CRS was measured, and did not report follow-up duration by intervention group. None of the included studies assessed adverse events. The authors concluded that polyclonal immunoglobulins appear to be beneficial in preventing rubella when compared to no treatment. The evidence suggests that the intervention is most effective when administered within five days of exposure and that the dose is a critical factor. For the subgroup receiving the highest volume of gamma-globulin, the absolute risk reduction was 266 cases per 1000 individuals, with a number needed to treat (NNT) of four. However, the studies did not standardize the measurement of rubella-specific antibodies in the immunoglobulin products, making it difficult to estimate the dose of rubella-specific antibodies in international units. As the concentration of rubella-specific antibodies in current immunoglobulin products may differ from those used in the studies, the required volume per pound of body weight to achieve similar results may also vary. There is insufficient evidence to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of polyclonal immunoglobulins in preventing congenital rubella syndrome. Further research is needed in this area.
